title: Fluorescent light fixture: tubes, ballast, diffuser panel and steel
summary: A fluorescent fixture gives you tubes (keep them whole), a heavy ballast, a translucent diffuser panel, painted steel and small starters. Allow about 20 minutes a fixture. The dangers are mercury in broken tubes, PCB oil in old ballasts, and mains wiring over your head on a ladder.

steps.text: Switch off the circuit at the breaker or fuse, not just the wall switch. With the grid down, a generator or solar system may still feed the building. Prove the fixture dead with a meter or tester at its wiring before you touch it (see safety_mains_isolation).
steps.warn: Fixtures are wired to mains and you will be working over your head. Never touch a wire you haven't proved dead.

steps.text: Stand a ladder on firm, level floor with a helper to steady it and take what you lower. Lay a blanket or cardboard underneath to catch anything that falls. Wear safety glasses, gloves and a hat.
steps.warn: Never lean sideways from a ladder. Climb down and move it.

steps.text: If the fixture has a lens, louvre or diffuser panel, take it off first. Troffer panels lift out of a hinged frame or sit in clips at the edges. They are thin and crack easily: lower each one flat to your helper.

Take the tubes out before you unbolt anything. Hold each tube by the middle and turn it a quarter turn in its sockets until the pins line up with the slots, then drop one end and slide it out of the other. Don't twist hard or let an end drop. Lay tubes flat in a cardboard box or wrapped in card, away from foot traffic. Dead tubes with black ends still hold their mercury.
steps.warn: Each tube holds a little mercury and phosphor powder inside thin glass. If one breaks, leave the room and open windows for 15 minutes; don't sweep or vacuum it (see the mercury hazard).

steps.text: Take off the cover plate over the ballast and wiring channel (screws, clips or twist tabs). Photograph the wiring before you touch anything. Check with the meter again that the supply wires are dead.

Disconnect the supply wires from the fixture: unscrew twist-on connectors anticlockwise or release the push-in terminals. Tape the end of each supply wire separately so it can't touch anything if the circuit is switched on again.

Have your helper hold the fixture while you undo its mountings: screws or toggle bolts into the ceiling, nuts on threaded rods, safety wires or T-bar clips. Lower it to the floor. Expect about 6 kg and sharp sheet-metal edges, so keep your gloves on.

Read the ballast label before you handle the ballast. 'No PCBs' printed on it, or a light flat electronic ballast with many thin wires, is safe to handle. A heavy magnetic ballast from before about 1980 with no 'No PCBs' label may hold PCB oil. If any ballast is leaking, oily, sticky or bulging, leave it sealed in the fixture, or bag it and keep it in a closed metal tin away from water.
steps.warn: PCB oil is toxic and never breaks down. Never cut open, drain, crush or burn a ballast, and never reuse the oil.

steps.text: A ballast that is fine to keep: wait at least 10 minutes after the power was switched off, cut its leads 10 cm from the case and undo its mounting screws. Magnetic ballasts weigh 1-2 kg and some have a small capacitor inside. Electronic ballasts hold a 400 V capacitor. Keep both whole and don't open them.
steps.warn: A ballast capacitor can hold a painful shock for days. Keep fingers off bare lead ends and the board until you have discharged it (see safety_discharge_capacitor).

steps.text: Twist out the starters (small aluminium or plastic cans beside each tube) a quarter turn anticlockwise and keep them as spares for older fixtures. If you want the tube sockets, cut their wires 5 cm from each and slide them out of their slots.
The steel body and reflector can stay whole or be cut up with a hacksaw. Wear gloves and file the cut edges. Stack the diffuser panels flat and wash off the dust.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Tubes.** Good tubes run in any fixture with the same pin base and a matching ballast. T12 tubes are 38 mm across, T8 are 26 mm and T5 are 16 mm. Match the tube to the label on the ballast (T12, T8 or T5, and watts), or it may flicker or die early. Store them flat or upright in a box, dry, and label the box 'mercury'. They will not run on 12 V DC without a special inverter ballast, as in caravan and boat lights.
- **Ballast.** A magnetic ballast is a heavy coil on an iron core that limits the current through the tube. Keep it with a matching tube to light a fixture again. Its copper and iron are worth recycling for someone who knows how to rewind a transformer. An electronic ballast is a small high-frequency inverter: keep it whole and use it as it was made.
- **Diffuser panels.** Prismatic acrylic or polystyrene, about 60 x 120 cm. Translucent glazing for a cold frame, a seedling cover or a window patch. Cut by scoring deeply with a knife along a straight edge and snapping it over a bench edge.
- **Steel housing and reflector.** Flat painted steel for patches, brackets and a drip tray. Polished aluminium louvres make good reflectors for a solar oven (see build_solar_oven).
- **Starters.** Spare glow-switch starters for older fixtures.

## Variations

- LED retrofit tubes (no mercury) look like plain plastic tubes and may be wired straight to the mains, with no ballast. Treat the fixture wiring as live until proved dead.
- Compact fluorescent bulbs hold mercury too: don't break them.
- Wet and outdoor fixtures have gaskets and are often full of water and insects; wear gloves and a mask.

## What to leave

- Broken tubes, and any floor they landed on: see the mercury hazard.
- Leaking or oily ballasts.
